screens.title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
screens.narratorSegment: Today we study the Interface Segregation Principle, or ISP, a SOLID guideline that asks a simple question: should a client depend on methods it never uses? ISP recommends designing interfaces from the client's point of view, keeping contracts lean and relevant. A common symptom of violating ISP is a fat interface: one large interface that forces implementers to provide empty or error-throwing methods. For example, a single Worker interface that mixes work, eat, sleep, and team management responsibilities will push a robot implementation to implement meaningless methods. That harms clarity, increases change impact, and makes testing harder. In practice, ISP means breaking a monolithic interface into smaller, role-focused interfaces such as Workable, Feedable, Sleepable, and Manageable, so each class implements only what it needs. This chapter shows concrete examples, a Python demonstration of a fat interface, a step-by-step refactoring pattern, and common mistakes to avoid—like creating tiny meaningless interfaces. As you go through the lesson, look for where responsibilities belong and ask: which client is this interface serving? That question will guide healthier, more maintainable designs.

keyIdea.title: Core Idea
keyIdea.text: Clients should only depend on the methods they actually use. Prefer several focused interfaces over one bloated interface.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will grasp the core idea behind the Interface Segregation Principle and why it reduces unnecessary coupling. You will be able to spot a fat interface in an object-oriented design by recognizing methods that do not belong together for all implementers. You will learn how ISP improves maintainability and testability by letting classes depend on narrower contracts, and you'll practice balancing interface size so you avoid both bloat and fragmentation. Each objective is practical: identifying violations helps you refactor code safely; understanding the rationale helps you prioritize which interfaces to split; and balancing granularity prevents creating many meaningless interfaces. For example, when a robot class is forced to implement sleep and manage_team methods, you will recognize that the interface serves mixed responsibilities and should be split into client-specific capabilities. Throughout the lessons you will see concrete Python examples, a hands-on refactor activity for a smart home system, and assessment questions that test whether you can both identify and apply ISP correctly. Keep these objectives in mind as diagnostic checks while you read and refactor.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice Focus
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on applying ISP in concrete code and tests. You will learn to refactor a fat interface by isolating client-specific capabilities, then update client code so it depends on the smaller interfaces. Practically, this reduces the chance of runtime errors from unsupported methods and shrinks the scope of changes when an interface evolves. You will also learn how narrower interfaces improve unit testing: mocks and fakes only need to implement the small contract the test cares about. During the hands-on smart home activity you will refactor a single SmartDevice interface into Switchable, Dimmable, TemperatureControllable, and DoorControllable interfaces so each device class implements just what it needs. Finally, you will practice writing client functions that accept the narrowest possible interface, ensuring they cannot call unsupported behavior. This reduces hidden coupling and keeps your code clearer. As you practice, ask: which methods belong together for a single role, and which belong to a distinct capability?

screens.title: What is the Interface Segregation Principle?
screens.narratorSegment: The Interface Segregation Principle states that clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. In other words, prefer several specific interfaces to one general-purpose interface that bundles unrelated methods. The rationale is practical: when an interface contains methods that many implementers don't need, those implementers either provide empty implementations or throw errors. That creates hidden coupling, increases change surface area, and reduces clarity about an interface's purpose. A helpful metaphor is a restaurant menu: a single menu listing every dish across appetizers, mains, desserts, and beverages forces a customer interested only in desserts to navigate unrelated options. Instead, separate menus for dessert, drinks, and entrees make choices clearer and prevent accidental dependencies. Similarly, client-specific interfaces present only the capabilities a client uses. A common misconception is that more interfaces always mean more complexity; the real point of ISP is useful focus. We want interfaces that represent coherent responsibilities so implementers naturally model the role's behavior, not arbitrary method collections. Consider whether every method on an interface is used by every client. If not, you likely need segregation.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: ISP: design interfaces so clients only see and depend on the methods they actually use.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › ISP Definition
What ISP claims
Clients should not be forced to implement or depend on methods they do not use. Interfaces should present a coherent, client-relevant contract.
Metaphor
Separate menus for specific needs, not one unwieldy menu for everything.
Common misconception
Many interfaces is not the goal; the goal is focused, cohesive contracts for clients.
Quick checklist to apply ISP
  • Ask which methods each client actually calls.
  • If many clients ignore some methods, consider splitting the interface.
  • Create interfaces that map to client roles or capabilities.
  • Avoid tiny meaningless interfaces; group related behaviors.
Key Takeaway

Design interfaces for the client's needs, not for the convenience of implementers or a single conceptual domain object.

screens.title: Fat Interface: symptoms and costs
screens.narratorSegment: A fat interface contains many methods that do not form a cohesive responsibility and as a result forces implementers and clients into problematic patterns. The most visible symptom is that some implementers provide empty method bodies or throw runtime errors for methods they cannot support. For example, when a MultiFunctionDevice lists print, scan, fax, and staple, a simple printer may implement only print and must either raise not implemented errors for the other methods or provide no-ops. This increases fragility: when the interface evolves and a new method is added, every implementer must change, even if the new method is irrelevant. That violates the spirit of the Open/Closed Principle by forcing modifications across the codebase. Fat interfaces also reduce clarity: developers cannot tell which subset of behaviors is relevant to a client by looking at the interface, and tests must mock or stub unnecessary methods. Finally, build and review costs increase because changes ripple across unrelated implementers and clients. The right solution is not always more interfaces, but clearer, client-centered segregation that groups truly related behaviors together. Do a quick audit: list clients, the methods they actually use, and split the interface where groups of methods are only used together.

keyIdea.text: Fat interfaces force stubbed or erroring implementations, increase change impact, and obscure the interface's real purpose.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Fat Interface
Symptoms
  • Implementers provide empty or error-throwing methods.
  • Clients depend on large contracts they only partially use.
  • Adding a method forces changes across many classes.
Fragility example
A single added method in a fat interface requires updates to all implementers, even those that never use it.
Costs
These issues increase coupling and make testing harder. Clients may fail at runtime if they call unsupported methods, and code reviews must consider unrelated behaviors when an interface changes.
Maintainability
More classes change after interface updates.
Testability
Mocks must implement unused methods, increasing test surface.

screens.title: Fat Interface in Python: MultiFunctionDevice
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete Python example that demonstrates a fat interface and the problems it creates. The MultiFunctionDevice abstract class declares print, scan, fax, and staple. A SimplePrinter implements only printing but is forced to stub or raise errors for scan, fax, and staple. An AdvancedPrinter provides all methods. The key observation is that SimplePrinter must expose methods it does not support, which may cause runtime errors when client code assumes a full-featured device. When you test or mock MultiFunctionDevice, you must handle methods unused by specific implementations, making tests more verbose and brittle. As you read the code, notice where the NotImplementedError appears and which class provides only the subset of behavior it truly needs. The remediation is to split the multi-function contract into focused interfaces—one for printing, one for scanning, and so on—so SimplePrinter implements only printing. That change keeps client functions safe: a function that needs only printing should type against the printable interface and will not accidentally call unsupported operations. Now examine the code block and highlight the methods you think belong to separate interfaces.

keyIdea.title: Code Insight
keyIdea.text: The provided Python example shows a MultiFunctionDevice interface forcing SimplePrinter to implement unsupported methods, a clear ISP violation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › MultiFunctionDevice
Fat interface example (Python)
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class MultiFunctionDevice(ABC):  # This is a fat interface
    @abstractmethod
    def print_document(self, document):
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def scan_document(self, document):
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def fax_document(self, document):
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def staple_document(self, document):
        pass

class SimplePrinter(MultiFunctionDevice):
    def print_document(self, document):
        print(f"Printing: {document}")

    def scan_document(self, document):
        raise NotImplementedError("SimplePrinter cannot scan.")

    def fax_document(self, document):
        raise NotImplementedError("SimplePrinter cannot fax.")

    def staple_document(self, document):
        raise NotImplementedError("SimplePrinter cannot staple.")

class AdvancedPrinter(MultiFunctionDevice):
    def print_document(self, document):
        print(f"Advanced Printing: {document}")

    def scan_document(self, document):
        print(f"Scanning: {document}")

    def fax_document(self, document):
        print(f"Faxing: {document}")

    def staple_document(self, document):
        print(f"Stapling: {document}")

def operate_printer(device: MultiFunctionDevice, doc):
    device.print_document(doc)
    # device.scan_document(doc)  # This would fail for SimplePrinter
Example observation
SimplePrinter raises NotImplementedError for unsupported methods, exposing an ISP violation.
Refactor hint
Split MultiFunctionDevice into IPrintable, IScannable, IFaxable, IStapleable interfaces.

screens.title: Refactoring pattern: split by client needs
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring a fat interface is a pragmatic, iterative process. Start by cataloging clients and listing exactly which methods each client actually calls. This empirical step prevents premature over-segmentation. Next, group methods into capability sets that align with client roles — for example, printing belongs with printing methods, scanning with scanning methods. Create new focused interfaces for each capability group and update implementers to implement only the interfaces they need. Then, change client code to depend on the narrowest interface required by their behavior. If a client needs multiple capabilities, it can depend on multiple small interfaces rather than a single large one. After refactoring, run tests and adjust mocks to the new contracts. A useful safety tip is to perform the change behind a compatibility adapter if needed: keep the old interface in place temporarily while migrating clients. A common pitfall is splitting based on convenience instead of actual client usage; to avoid that, use your initial client audit as the final authority. This process reduces unnecessary methods on implementers and narrows the surface area of change. Refactoring pattern: split by client needs means audit clients → group methods by capability → create focused interfaces → update implementers and clients → test and iterate.. In practical terms, step-by-step approach to segregate an interface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Audit clients → group methods by capability → create focused interfaces → update implementers and clients → test and iterate.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Refactor Pattern
Segregation process
  1. Audit clients: list which methods each client calls in practice.
  2. Group capabilities: cluster methods that are used together by clients.
  3. Create focused interfaces: one interface per capability set.
  4. Update implementers: implement only the interfaces they need.
  5. Migrate clients: change client signatures to accept narrow interfaces.
  6. Test and adapt: run tests and iterate until behavior is stable.
Concrete example
From MultiFunctionDevice create IPrintable (print), IScannable (scan), IFaxable (fax), IStapleable (staple). Update SimplePrinter to implement only IPrintable.
Pro Tip

Make the smallest change first: add a new small interface, migrate a single implementer, and then update clients one at a time.

screens.title: How ISP improves decoupling and maintainability
screens.narratorSegment: Segregating interfaces has direct architectural benefits. When clients depend only on focused interfaces, coupling is reduced because changes to one capability do not ripple into unrelated clients. For example, adding a new method to a stapling interface will only affect implementers and clients concerned with stapling, leaving printing clients untouched. This narrows the blast radius of changes and makes code easier to reason about. Testability improves because unit tests mock the small interface the test needs rather than a bulky contract with many irrelevant methods. From a dependency perspective, components now depend on behavior, not on a monolithic type that mixes responsibilities. This supports cleaner substitution and makes it easier to introduce adapters or facades for specific capabilities. One misconception is to think ISP reduces reuse: in fact, focused interfaces make it clearer which capabilities can be reused independently. The practical rule is to design interfaces around coherent responsibilities and let classes compose multiple small interfaces if they provide several capabilities. This leads to a more modular, maintainable architecture. How ISP improves decoupling and maintainability means isp reduces change impact, improves testability, and clarifies component dependencies by narrowing interface contracts.. In practical terms, the architectural benefits of client-specific interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Benefits at a glance
Reduced blast radius
Changes to one capability affect only related clients and implementers.
Better testability
Mocks only implement required methods, simplifying unit tests.
Clearer dependencies

Key Takeaway

screens.title: Avoid interface explosion
screens.narratorSegment: While ISP promotes smaller interfaces, a common mistake is to take segregation too far and create many tiny, meaningless interfaces. This is often called interface explosion. The result is anemic contracts that force implementers and clients to depend on many tiny interfaces, which can increase surface area and cognitive overhead. The balance point is to design interfaces that represent coherent capabilities — groups of related behaviors that make sense together for a client role. For instance, grouping all brightness-related methods into a Dimmable interface makes sense for lights, while an unrelated temperature method should sit in a separate TemperatureControllable interface. Use your client audit to guide decisions: if two methods are always used together by the same set of clients, keep them in one interface. If they serve distinct roles, separate them. Also prefer naming that communicates a role or capability so interfaces remain meaningful. The goal is to reduce coupling and improve clarity, not to maximize the number of interfaces. Avoid interface explosion means create interfaces that model meaningful capabilities; avoid splitting until each interface still represents a useful contract.. In practical terms, finding balance between bloat and fragmentation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Avoid splitting too far
Too many tiny interfaces
Leads to higher coupling by forcing clients to assemble many small contracts.
Good granularity
Interfaces represent a coherent capability used by one or more clients.
Decision rule: Keep methods together if the same set of clients uses them; split when clients diverge in usage.

fullNarratorScript:
Today we study the Interface Segregation Principle, or ISP, a SOLID guideline that asks a simple question: should a client depend on methods it never uses? ISP recommends designing interfaces from the client's point of view, keeping contracts lean and relevant. A common symptom of violating ISP is a fat interface: one large interface that forces implementers to provide empty or error-throwing methods. For example, a single Worker interface that mixes work, eat, sleep, and team management responsibilities will push a robot implementation to implement meaningless methods. That harms clarity, increases change impact, and makes testing harder. In practice, ISP means breaking a monolithic interface into smaller, role-focused interfaces such as Workable, Feedable, Sleepable, and Manageable, so each class implements only what it needs. This chapter shows concrete examples, a Python demonstration of a fat interface, a step-by-step refactoring pattern, and common mistakes to avoid—like creating tiny meaningless interfaces. As you go through the lesson, look for where responsibilities belong and ask: which client is this interface serving? That question will guide healthier, more maintainable designs.

By the end of this chapter you will grasp the core idea behind the Interface Segregation Principle and why it reduces unnecessary coupling. You will be able to spot a fat interface in an object-oriented design by recognizing methods that do not belong together for all implementers. You will learn how ISP improves maintainability and testability by letting classes depend on narrower contracts, and you'll practice balancing interface size so you avoid both bloat and fragmentation. Each objective is practical: identifying violations helps you refactor code safely; understanding the rationale helps you prioritize which interfaces to split; and balancing granularity prevents creating many meaningless interfaces. For example, when a robot class is forced to implement sleep and manage_team methods, you will recognize that the interface serves mixed responsibilities and should be split into client-specific capabilities. Throughout the lessons you will see concrete Python examples, a hands-on refactor activity for a smart home system, and assessment questions that test whether you can both identify and apply ISP correctly. Keep these objectives in mind as diagnostic checks while you read and refactor.

These objectives focus on applying ISP in concrete code and tests. You will learn to refactor a fat interface by isolating client-specific capabilities, then update client code so it depends on the smaller interfaces. Practically, this reduces the chance of runtime errors from unsupported methods and shrinks the scope of changes when an interface evolves. You will also learn how narrower interfaces improve unit testing: mocks and fakes only need to implement the small contract the test cares about. During the hands-on smart home activity you will refactor a single SmartDevice interface into Switchable, Dimmable, TemperatureControllable, and DoorControllable interfaces so each device class implements just what it needs. Finally, you will practice writing client functions that accept the narrowest possible interface, ensuring they cannot call unsupported behavior. This reduces hidden coupling and keeps your code clearer. As you practice, ask: which methods belong together for a single role, and which belong to a distinct capability?

The Interface Segregation Principle states that clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. In other words, prefer several specific interfaces to one general-purpose interface that bundles unrelated methods. The rationale is practical: when an interface contains methods that many implementers don't need, those implementers either provide empty implementations or throw errors. That creates hidden coupling, increases change surface area, and reduces clarity about an interface's purpose. A helpful metaphor is a restaurant menu: a single menu listing every dish across appetizers, mains, desserts, and beverages forces a customer interested only in desserts to navigate unrelated options. Instead, separate menus for dessert, drinks, and entrees make choices clearer and prevent accidental dependencies. Similarly, client-specific interfaces present only the capabilities a client uses. A common misconception is that more interfaces always mean more complexity; the real point of ISP is useful focus. We want interfaces that represent coherent responsibilities so implementers naturally model the role's behavior, not arbitrary method collections. Consider whether every method on an interface is used by every client. If not, you likely need segregation.

A fat interface contains many methods that do not form a cohesive responsibility and as a result forces implementers and clients into problematic patterns. The most visible symptom is that some implementers provide empty method bodies or throw runtime errors for methods they cannot support. For example, when a MultiFunctionDevice lists print, scan, fax, and staple, a simple printer may implement only print and must either raise not implemented errors for the other methods or provide no-ops. This increases fragility: when the interface evolves and a new method is added, every implementer must change, even if the new method is irrelevant. That violates the spirit of the Open/Closed Principle by forcing modifications across the codebase. Fat interfaces also reduce clarity: developers cannot tell which subset of behaviors is relevant to a client by looking at the interface, and tests must mock or stub unnecessary methods. Finally, build and review costs increase because changes ripple across unrelated implementers and clients. The right solution is not always more interfaces, but clearer, client-centered segregation that groups truly related behaviors together. Do a quick audit: list clients, the methods they actually use, and split the interface where groups of methods are only used together.

Let's walk through a concrete Python example that demonstrates a fat interface and the problems it creates. The MultiFunctionDevice abstract class declares print, scan, fax, and staple. A SimplePrinter implements only printing but is forced to stub or raise errors for scan, fax, and staple. An AdvancedPrinter provides all methods. The key observation is that SimplePrinter must expose methods it does not support, which may cause runtime errors when client code assumes a full-featured device. When you test or mock MultiFunctionDevice, you must handle methods unused by specific implementations, making tests more verbose and brittle. As you read the code, notice where the NotImplementedError appears and which class provides only the subset of behavior it truly needs. The remediation is to split the multi-function contract into focused interfaces—one for printing, one for scanning, and so on—so SimplePrinter implements only printing. That change keeps client functions safe: a function that needs only printing should type against the printable interface and will not accidentally call unsupported operations. Now examine the code block and highlight the methods you think belong to separate interfaces.

Refactoring a fat interface is a pragmatic, iterative process. Start by cataloging clients and listing exactly which methods each client actually calls. This empirical step prevents premature over-segmentation. Next, group methods into capability sets that align with client roles — for example, printing belongs with printing methods, scanning with scanning methods. Create new focused interfaces for each capability group and update implementers to implement only the interfaces they need. Then, change client code to depend on the narrowest interface required by their behavior. If a client needs multiple capabilities, it can depend on multiple small interfaces rather than a single large one. After refactoring, run tests and adjust mocks to the new contracts. A useful safety tip is to perform the change behind a compatibility adapter if needed: keep the old interface in place temporarily while migrating clients. A common pitfall is splitting based on convenience instead of actual client usage; to avoid that, use your initial client audit as the final authority. This process reduces unnecessary methods on implementers and narrows the surface area of change. Refactoring pattern: split by client needs means audit clients → group methods by capability → create focused interfaces → update implementers and clients → test and iterate.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Segregating interfaces has direct architectural benefits. When clients depend only on focused interfaces, coupling is reduced because changes to one capability do not ripple into unrelated clients. For example, adding a new method to a stapling interface will only affect implementers and clients concerned with stapling, leaving printing clients untouched. This narrows the blast radius of changes and makes code easier to reason about. Testability improves because unit tests mock the small interface the test needs rather than a bulky contract with many irrelevant methods. From a dependency perspective, components now depend on behavior, not on a monolithic type that mixes responsibilities. This supports cleaner substitution and makes it easier to introduce adapters or facades for specific capabilities. One misconception is to think ISP reduces reuse: in fact, focused interfaces make it clearer which capabilities can be reused independently. The practical rule is to design interfaces around coherent responsibilities and let classes compose multiple small interfaces if they provide several capabilities. This leads to a more modular, maintainable architecture. While ISP promotes smaller interfaces, a common mistake is to take segregation too far and create many tiny, meaningless interfaces. This is often called interface explosion. The result is anemic contracts that force implementers and clients to depend on many tiny interfaces, which can increase surface area and cognitive overhead. The balance point is to design interfaces that represent coherent capabilities — groups of related behaviors that make sense together for a client role. For instance, grouping all brightness-related methods into a Dimmable interface makes sense for lights, while an unrelated temperature method should sit in a separate TemperatureControllable interface. Use your client audit to guide decisions: if two methods are always used together by the same set of clients, keep them in one interface. If they serve distinct roles, separate them. Also prefer naming that communicates a role or capability so interfaces remain meaningful. The goal is to reduce coupling and improve clarity, not to maximize the number of interfaces. Avoid interface explosion means create interfaces that model meaningful capabilities; avoid splitting until each interface still represents a useful contract..
